questions.q: Which sensory modalities are carried by the Dorsal Column-Medial Lemniscus (DCML) pathway, where do its first-order and second-order neurons synapse, and where do its axons decussate?
options: Fine discriminative touch, vibration, conscious proprioception, and two-point discrimination; first-order neurons ascend ipsilaterally in the fasciculus gracilis (T7 and below) and fasciculus cuneatus (T6 and above) to synapse in the nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus in the caudal medulla; second-order internal arcuate fibers decussate in the caudal medulla and ascend as the medial lemniscus to the thalamic VPL nucleus
Pain, temperature, and crude touch; second-order axons decussate in the spinal cord anterior white commissure
Unconscious proprioception from muscle spindles directly to the cerebellar cortex
Visceral taste and baroreceptor signals to the hypothalamus
questions.explain: Because the DCML pathway decussates in the caudal medulla, a spinal cord hemisection causes ipsilateral loss of vibration/proprioception below the lesion, whereas a thalamic or cortical stroke causes contralateral loss.

open.q: State the sensory modalities, first-order synaptic nuclei, site of decussation, and thalamic relay nucleus of the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway.
accept: Fine touch, vibration, conscious proprioception, two-point discrimination; nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus; decussates as internal arcuate fibers in the caudal medulla; ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus
Fine touch/vibration/proprioception; gracilis & cuneatus nuclei; caudal medulla; thalamic VPL

questions.q: How does the Anterolateral System (spinothalamic tract) differ from the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway in its level of decussation and sensory modalities?
options: It transmits pain, temperature, and crude/non-discriminative touch; primary A-delta and C afferents enter the dorsal horn, ascend 1-2 segments in Lissauer's tract, synapse in substantia gelatinosa/nucleus proprius, and second-order axons decussate immediately in the spinal cord anterior white commissure to ascend contralaterally to the thalamic VPL nucleus
It carries conscious proprioception and decussates in the midbrain superior colliculus
It ascends uncrossed all the way to the ipsilateral primary somatosensory cortex
It carries motor commands from Betz cells to ventral horn alpha motor neurons
questions.explain: Early spinal decussation (1-2 segments above entry) explains why unilateral spinal cord hemisection causes contralateral loss of pain and temperature starting 1-2 dermatomes below the lesion.

open.q: Compare the site of decussation and sensory modalities of the lateral spinothalamic tract versus the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway.
accept: Spinothalamic: pain and temperature, decussates in the spinal cord anterior white commissure (1-2 segments above entry); Dorsal columns: fine touch, vibration, conscious proprioception, decussates in the caudal medulla
Pain/temperature crossing in spinal cord anterior white commissure vs fine touch/vibration/proprioception crossing in caudal medulla

questions.q: How do the dorsal (posterior) spinocerebellar tract and ventral (anterior) spinocerebellar tract differ in their spinal origin, crossing pattern, and cerebellar peduncle of entry?
options: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract arises from Clarke's nucleus (C8-L2), remains ENTIRELY IPSILATERAL, and enters the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle; Ventral spinocerebellar tract arises from lumbosacral spinal border cells, crosses TWICE (decussates in the spinal cord and re-crosses in the superior cerebellar peduncle) to end IPSILATERALLY in the cerebellum
Both tracts terminate in the contralateral primary visual cortex
Dorsal spinocerebellar tract crosses three times in the pons
Ventral spinocerebellar tract carries conscious pain from the face
questions.explain: Because the ventral spinocerebellar tract double-crosses while the dorsal spinocerebellar tract never crosses, BOTH tracts deliver ipsilateral unconscious proprioceptive information to the same cerebellar hemisphere!

open.q: Explain why lesions of one cerebellar hemisphere produce ipsilateral rather than contralateral ataxia with respect to spinocerebellar tract decussation.
accept: Dorsal spinocerebellar fibers remain uncrossed (ipsilateral) and ventral spinocerebellar fibers cross twice (in the spinal cord and again in the superior cerebellar peduncle), so both terminate in the ipsilateral cerebellum
Dorsal is uncrossed and ventral double-crosses, giving each cerebellar hemisphere ipsilateral body representation

questions.q: Compare the decussation, spinal cord termination, and primary motor functions of the Lateral Corticospinal Tract versus the Anterior (Ventral) Corticospinal Tract:
options: Lateral corticospinal tract (~85-90% of pyramidal fibers) decussates in the caudal medullary pyramids and synapses on lateral ventral horn neurons controlling skilled, fractionated distal limb movements; Anterior corticospinal tract (~10-15%) descends ipsilaterally in the anterior funiculus and decussates at the segmental spinal level via the anterior white commissure to control bilateral axial and proximal girdle muscles
Lateral corticospinal tract controls only eye movements; anterior controls tongue protrusion
Anterior corticospinal tract decussates in the midbrain and controls finger dexterity
Both tracts originate exclusively in the cerebellar dentate nucleus
questions.explain: Bilateral segmental projection of the anterior corticospinal tract explains why axial/trunk muscles are relatively spared in a unilateral hemispheric stroke.

open.q: State the percentage of fibers, site of decussation, and primary muscle groups controlled by the lateral corticospinal tract versus the anterior corticospinal tract.
accept: Lateral (~85-90%): decussates in caudal medulla, controls distal limb muscles; Anterior (~10-15%): decussates segmentally in the spinal cord, controls axial/proximal trunk muscles
Lateral: 85-90%, medullary decussation, distal limbs; Anterior: 10-15%, segmental spinal decussation, axial/proximal muscles

questions.q: How do the medial brainstem descending motor pathways (vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts) differ functionally from the lateral descending motor pathways (lateral corticospinal and rubrospinal tracts)?
options: Medial pathways (lateral/medial vestibulospinal and pontine/medullary reticulospinal) terminate in the ventromedial spinal gray to maintain upright posture, balance, and antigravity extensor tone; Lateral pathways (lateral corticospinal and rubrospinal) terminate in the dorsolateral ventral horn to control skilled distal limb movement and flexor tone
Vestibulospinal tracts innervate only facial expression muscles
Rubrospinal tract arises in the lumbar spinal cord and ascends to the cortex
Medial pathways control independent piano-playing finger movements
questions.explain: Specifically, the lateral vestibulospinal tract (from Deiters' lateral vestibular nucleus) and pontine reticulospinal tract strongly excite antigravity extensor motor neurons, whereas the medullary reticulospinal tract inhibits extensor tone.

open.q: Contrast the functional roles of the lateral vestibulospinal tract and rubrospinal tract on extensor versus flexor motor neurons.
accept: Lateral vestibulospinal tract excites antigravity extensor motor neurons (posture/balance); Rubrospinal tract facilitates upper-limb flexor motor neurons and inhibits extensors
Vestibulospinal excites extensors; rubrospinal excites upper-limb flexors

questions.sub: Spinal Cord Laminae and Blood Supply
questions.q: Which spinal cord tracts and gray matter columns are supplied by the single Anterior Spinal Artery versus the paired Posterior Spinal Arteries, and what is the clinical triad of Anterior Spinal Artery occlusion?
options: Anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the cord (ventral horns, lateral corticospinal tracts, spinothalamic tracts, intermediolateral cell column), so occlusion causes bilateral motor paralysis, bilateral loss of pain and temperature below the lesion, and autonomic bladder/bowel dysfunction, WITH complete sparing of vibration and proprioception (supplied by the paired posterior spinal arteries)
Anterior spinal artery supplies only the dorsal columns; occlusion causes pure loss of vibration
Posterior spinal arteries supply the ventral horns; occlusion causes pure flaccid paralysis
Anterior spinal artery occlusion affects only the face and tongue
questions.explain: Dissociated sensory loss (absent pain/temperature with preserved vibration/proprioception) plus bilateral motor paralysis below the lesion is pathognomonic for Anterior Spinal Artery syndrome (often due to aortic cross-clamping or artery of Adamkiewicz occlusion).

open.q: List the neurological deficits and the specific sensory modalities spared in Anterior Spinal Artery occlusion.
accept: Deficits: bilateral motor paralysis (UMN below, LMN at lesion level), bilateral loss of pain and temperature below the lesion, and autonomic sphincter loss; Spared: vibration, conscious proprioception, and fine touch (dorsal columns)
Bilateral paralysis + loss of pain/temperature + sphincter dysfunction, with spared dorsal column vibration and proprioception

questions.sub: Brainstem Anatomy, Cranial Nerve Nuclei, and Rule of 4s
questions.q: How are cranial nerve nuclei organized embryologically from medial to lateral across the sulcus limitans in the brainstem tegmentum?
options: Motor (efferent) nuclei lie MEDIAL to the sulcus limitans (from medial to lateral: General Somatic Efferent [GSE: CN III, IV, VI, XII], Special Visceral/Branchial Efferent [SVE: CN V, VII, nucleus ambiguus IX/X/XI], General Visceral Efferent parasympathetic [GVE: Edinger-Westphal, superior/inferior salivatory, dorsal motor nucleus of X]); Sensory (afferent) nuclei lie LATERAL to the sulcus limitans (visceral afferent [NTS] medial, somatic/special sensory [trigeminal, vestibular, cochlear] lateral)
Sensory nuclei lie strictly on the ventral surface of the pyramids; motor nuclei lie in the fourth ventricle roof
All cranial nerve nuclei are located in the cervical spinal cord
Parasympathetic nuclei lie lateral to the cochlear nuclei
questions.explain: Embryological basal plate (medial = motor) vs alar plate (lateral = sensory) organization underpins the clinical 'Rule of 4s' for brainstem stroke localization.

open.q: State the embryological rule governing the medial-to-lateral arrangement of motor versus sensory cranial nerve nuclei relative to the sulcus limitans.
accept: Motor (efferent) nuclei derived from the basal plate lie medial to the sulcus limitans (GSE most medial, SVE intermediate, GVE lateral), whereas sensory (afferent) nuclei derived from the alar plate lie lateral to the sulcus limitans
Motor nuclei medial to sulcus limitans; sensory nuclei lateral to sulcus limitans

questions.sub: Brainstem Anatomy, Cranial Nerve Nuclei, and Rule of 4s
questions.q: What are the classic clinical features of 'Lateral Medullary (Wallenberg) Syndrome' caused by occlusion of the vertebral artery or Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA)?
options: 1) Dysphagia, hoarseness, and absent gag reflex (ipsilateral nucleus ambiguus CN IX/X); 2) Loss of pain & temperature on IPSILATERAL face (spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract) and CONTRALATERAL body (spinothalamic tract); 3) Vertigo, nausea, vomiting, nystagmus (vestibular nuclei); 4) Ipsilateral limb ataxia (inferior cerebellar peduncle); 5) Ipsilateral Horner syndrome (descending hypothalamospinal sympathetic fibers)
Ipsilateral tongue paralysis (CN XII) and contralateral spastic hemiparesis with loss of vibration
Bilateral blindness and anosmia
Pure upward gaze paralysis and light-near dissociation
questions.explain: Dysphagia and hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus) specifically distinguish lateral medullary (PICA/vertebral) infarction from lateral pontine (AICA) infarction (which instead affects CN VII and CN VIII).

open.q: List four classic neurological deficits of Lateral Medullary (Wallenberg) Syndrome and match each to its damaged brainstem structure.
accept: 1) Dysphagia/hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus); 2) Ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss (spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract); 3) Contralateral body pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic tract); 4) Vertigo/nystagmus (vestibular nuclei); 5) Ipsilateral ataxia (inferior cerebellar peduncle); 6) Ipsilateral Horner syndrome (descending sympathetic tract)
Nucleus ambiguus (dysphagia/hoarseness), spinal V (ipsilateral facial pain/temp), spinothalamic (contralateral body pain/temp), inferior cerebellar peduncle (ataxia), sympathetic fibers (Horner)

questions.sub: Brainstem Anatomy, Cranial Nerve Nuclei, and Rule of 4s
questions.q: What is the clinical triad of 'Medial Medullary (Dejerine) Syndrome' caused by occlusion of paramedian branches of the anterior spinal or vertebral artery?
options: 1) Contralateral spastic hemiparesis of arm and leg (medullary pyramid / corticospinal tract); 2) Contralateral loss of vibration and conscious proprioception (medial lemniscus); 3) Ipsilateral lower motor neuron tongue paralysis with tongue deviation TOWARD the side of the lesion on protrusion (hypoglossal nerve CN XII)
Ipsilateral facial droop, deafness, and vertigo
Dysphagia, hoarseness, and ipsilateral Horner syndrome
Bilateral ptosis and fixed dilated pupils
questions.explain: Remember the midline 'M' structures of the medulla: Motor pathway (pyramid), Medial lemniscus, and Motor nucleus/nerve of CN XII (tongue).

open.q: State the three classic neurological findings of Medial Medullary Syndrome and the affected structure for each.
accept: 1) Contralateral hemiparesis (medullary pyramid/corticospinal tract); 2) Contralateral loss of vibration/proprioception (medial lemniscus); 3) Ipsilateral tongue weakness/atrophy deviating toward the lesion (hypoglossal nerve CN XII)
Pyramid (contralateral weakness), medial lemniscus (contralateral proprioception/vibration loss), CN XII (ipsilateral tongue deviation)

questions.sub: Brainstem Anatomy, Cranial Nerve Nuclei, and Rule of 4s
questions.q: What is 'Locked-In Syndrome', which brainstem vascular occlusion or metabolic injury causes it, and which functions remain intact?
options: Infarction of the ventral basis pontis (basilar artery thrombosis) or central pontine myelinolysis destroys bilateral corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts (causing complete quadriplegia and loss of speech/swallowing/horizontal eye movements), while sparing the dorsal pontine/midbrain tegmental Ascending Reticular Activating System (ARAS) and vertical gaze pathways—leaving the patient fully conscious and able to communicate via vertical eye movements and blinking
Bilateral cortical death leaving the patient completely unconscious with intact motor reflexes
Selective lesion of the cerebellar vermis causing wide-based gait
Occlusion of the left anterior cerebral artery causing right leg weakness
questions.explain: Because the dorsal tegmental ARAS and midbrain vertical gaze centers (rostral interstitial MLF / CN III/IV) are spared, patients have intact cognition and vertical blinking/gaze.

open.q: Which brainstem region and tracts are destroyed versus spared in Locked-In Syndrome?
accept: Destroyed: ventral pons (basis pontis) containing bilateral corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts (quadriplegia and mutism); Spared: dorsal pontine/midbrain tegmentum (ARAS) and vertical eye movement centers (consciousness and vertical gaze/blinking preserved)
Ventral pons/corticospinal & corticobulbar destroyed; dorsal tegmental ARAS and vertical gaze spared

questions.sub: Reticular Formation, ARAS, and Decorticate vs Decerebrate Posturing
questions.q: What is the 'Ascending Reticular Activating System' (ARAS), where is it located, and what results from bilateral damage to this system?
options: A diffuse network of cholinergic, noradrenergic (locus coeruleus), serotonergic (raphe), histaminergic, and glutamatergic neurons in the rostral pontine and midbrain reticular core projecting via intralaminar thalamic nuclei to the entire cerebral cortex to maintain wakefulness and arousal; bilateral damage produces coma
A descending spinal tract that inhibits the patellar tendon reflex
A cerebellar nucleus that regulates fine finger coordination
A basal ganglia loop that releases dopamine into the CSF
questions.explain: Coma requires either bilateral diffuse cerebral cortical dysfunction OR a lesion interrupting the brainstem ARAS at or above the rostral pons.

open.q: State the anatomical location, thalamic relay, and primary physiological function of the Ascending Reticular Activating System (ARAS).
accept: Rostral pontine and midbrain reticular formation; projects through intralaminar thalamic nuclei (and basal forebrain/hypothalamus) to diffusely activate the cerebral cortex and maintain wakefulness/consciousness
Rostral pons/midbrain reticular core -> intralaminar thalamus -> cortex; maintains cortical arousal and consciousness

questions.sub: Reticular Formation, ARAS, and Decorticate vs Decerebrate Posturing
questions.q: How do 'decorticate posturing' and 'decerebrate posturing' differ in limb position, brainstem lesion level relative to the red nucleus, and clinical prognosis?
options: Decorticate posturing (lesion ABOVE the midbrain red nucleus, e.g., cerebral hemispheres/internal capsule): flexion of elbows, wrists, and fingers ('arms pulled to core') with extension/internal rotation of legs, because the intact red nucleus drives rubrospinal upper-limb flexion; Decerebrate posturing (lesion AT OR BELOW the red nucleus, e.g., midbrain/rostral pons): rigid extension, adduction, and internal rotation of BOTH arms and legs due to unopposed vestibulospinal/pontine reticulospinal extensor drive, carrying a worse prognosis
Decorticate posturing shows extension of all four limbs; decerebrate shows flexion of arms
Decerebrate posturing indicates a benign peripheral radial nerve injury
Both postures occur during normal stage N3 slow-wave sleep
questions.explain: Mnemonic: 'DeCORticate = arms flexed toward the CORe' (lesion above red nucleus; rubrospinal tract intact); 'DeCErebRate = all E's / Extended' (lesion at/below red nucleus; rubrospinal tract lost).

open.q: Contrast the arm posture and neuroanatomical lesion level (relative to the midbrain red nucleus) of decorticate versus decerebrate rigidity.
accept: Decorticate: flexed upper extremities and extended lower extremities; lesion above the red nucleus (intact rubrospinal flexor drive to arms); Decerebrate: rigid extension of both upper and lower extremities; lesion at or below the red nucleus (loss of rubrospinal drive, unopposed vestibulospinal/reticulospinal extensor tone)
Arms flexed, lesion above red nucleus (decorticate) vs arms & legs extended, lesion at/below red nucleus (decerebrate)

questions.q: Match the three functional/phylogenetic divisions of the cerebellum with their corresponding deep cerebellar nuclei and primary functions:
options: 1) Vestibulocerebellum (archicerebellum / flocculonodular lobe) -> vestibular nuclei -> balance, equilibrium, and vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR); 2) Spinocerebellum (paleocerebellum / vermis & intermediate paravermal hemisphere) -> fastigial & interposed (globose + emboliform) nuclei -> axial posture, gait, and real-time error correction of ongoing limb movement; 3) Cerebrocerebellum (neocerebellum / lateral hemispheres) -> dentate nucleus -> motor planning, timing, and coordination of skilled distal movements
Flocculonodular lobe -> dentate nucleus -> language comprehension
Lateral hemispheres -> fastigial nucleus -> pupillary light reflex
Vermis -> substantia nigra -> dopamine synthesis
questions.explain: Mnemonic for deep cerebellar nuclei from lateral to medial: 'Don't Eat Greasy Food' = Dentate, Emboliform, Globose (together = Interposed), Fastigial.

open.q: Match the three functional divisions of the cerebellum (vestibulocerebellum, spinocerebellum, cerebrocerebellum) with their anatomical regions, output nuclei, and primary functions.
accept: Vestibulocerebellum: flocculonodular lobe -> vestibular nuclei (balance & VOR); Spinocerebellum: vermis & paravermis -> fastigial & interposed nuclei (posture, gait & ongoing movement execution); Cerebrocerebellum: lateral hemispheres -> dentate nucleus (motor planning & skilled distal coordination)
Flocculonodular/vestibular (balance/eye movements), vermis-paravermis/fastigial-interposed (gait/ongoing movement), lateral hemispheres/dentate (motor planning)

questions.sub: Cerebellar Microcircuitry: Purkinje, Granule, Climbing, and Mossy Fibers
questions.q: In the cerebellar cortex, which cell type provides the SOLE axonal output from the cerebellar cortex, and what is its neurotransmitter and postsynaptic effect on the deep cerebellar nuclei?
options: Purkinje cells; they release GABA and exert a purely INHIBITORY effect on the deep cerebellar nuclei (and vestibular nuclei)
Granule cells; they release acetylcholine to excite the spinal cord directly
Basket cells; they release dopamine to excite the thalamus
Golgi cells; they release norepinephrine to inhibit the hippocampus
questions.explain: Every single axon leaving the cerebellar cortex is a GABAergic inhibitory Purkinje cell axon; the deep cerebellar nuclei themselves receive excitatory collaterals from mossy/climbing fibers and send excitatory glutamatergic output to brainstem and thalamus.

open.q: Name the sole output neuron of the cerebellar cortex, its neurotransmitter, and whether it excites or inhibits the deep cerebellar nuclei.
accept: Purkinje cell; GABA; inhibits the deep cerebellar nuclei
Purkinje cell; inhibitory (GABA)

questions.sub: Cerebellar Microcircuitry: Purkinje, Granule, Climbing, and Mossy Fibers
questions.q: How do 'climbing fibers' and 'mossy fibers' differ in their anatomical origin, synaptic connection onto Purkinje cells, and role in cerebellar motor learning?
options: Climbing fibers arise EXCLUSIVELY from the contralateral inferior olivary nucleus, wrap directly around a single Purkinje cell dendritic tree (1:1 ratio), and trigger powerful 'complex spikes' that signal motor error and induce long-term depression (LTD) at parallel fiber-Purkinje synapses; Mossy fibers arise from all other sources (spinocerebellar, pontocerebellar, vestibulocerebellar), synapse on granule cells (whose parallel fibers excite thousands of Purkinje cells), and evoke 'simple spikes'
Climbing fibers originate in the spinal dorsal horn and inhibit granule cells
Mossy fibers arise exclusively from the inferior olive and synapse 1:1 on Purkinje cells
Both climbing and mossy fibers release glycine to silence Purkinje cells
questions.explain: Climbing fiber error signals from the inferior olive drive cerebellar motor learning (such as adapting VOR gain or refining a tennis swing) by depressing erroneous parallel fiber inputs onto Purkinje cells.

open.q: Contrast climbing fibers and mossy fibers in terms of their anatomical origin and how they excite Purkinje cells.
accept: Climbing fibers: originate exclusively from the contralateral inferior olivary nucleus, synapse directly 1:1 on Purkinje cell dendrites, and generate complex spikes (error signals); Mossy fibers: originate from spinal, pontine, and vestibular nuclei, synapse on granule cells whose parallel fibers excite many Purkinje cells to generate simple spikes
Contralateral inferior olive -> direct 1:1 complex spikes (climbing) vs pontine/spinal/vestibular nuclei -> granule cell parallel fibers -> simple spikes (mossy)

questions.sub: Cerebellar Peduncles and Clinical Cerebellar Signs
questions.q: Which cerebellar peduncle carries the primary EFFERENT output of the cerebellum (from dentate and interposed nuclei to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamic VL nucleus), and why do unilateral cerebellar hemisphere lesions produce IPSILATERAL motor deficits?
options: Superior cerebellar peduncle (brachium conjunctivum); its efferent fibers decussate in the caudal midbrain to synapse in the contralateral red nucleus and VL thalamus -> contralateral motor cortex, whose corticospinal tract then decussates AGAIN in the caudal medulla—producing double decussation and ipsilateral clinical signs
Middle cerebellar peduncle (brachium pontis); it carries all cerebellar efferents to the spinal cord
Inferior cerebellar peduncle (restiform body); it carries corticopontocerebellar afferents exclusively
Cerebellar lesions cause contralateral paralysis because cerebellar axons never cross
questions.explain: Mnemonic: 'Middle = Motor input (pontocerebellar afferents only); Superior = Sending output (primary efferent peduncle).' Double crossing (superior cerebellar peduncle + medullary pyramids) means right cerebellum controls right limbs!

open.q: Identify the major fiber tracts passing through each of the three cerebellar peduncles (inferior, middle, superior) and explain why cerebellar signs are ipsilateral.
accept: Inferior: afferents from spinal cord (dorsal spinocerebellar), vestibular nuclei, and inferior olive (climbing fibers); Middle: afferents exclusively from contralateral pontine nuclei (pontocerebellar); Superior: primary cerebellar efferents (dentate/interposed -> contralateral red nucleus & VL thalamus); double decussation (SCP + corticospinal decussation) produces ipsilateral signs
Inferior (spinocerebellar/olivary/vestibular afferents), Middle (pontocerebellar afferents), Superior (dentatorubrothalamic efferents); double crossing yields ipsilateral signs

questions.sub: Cerebellar Peduncles and Clinical Cerebellar Signs
questions.q: Match the classic clinical signs of cerebellar hemisphere dysfunction (mnemonic 'VANISHED' / 'DANISH') with their definitions:
options: Dysmetria: inability to judge distance/range of movement (overshooting/past-pointing or undershooting on finger-to-nose test); Dysdiadochokinesia: inability to perform rapid alternating pronation-supination movements; Intention tremor: oscillating tremor that worsens as the limb approaches a target; Scanning dysarthria: slow, slurred, staccato speech with irregular syllable emphasis; Hypotonia and pendular knee jerk
Resting pill-rolling tremor, lead-pipe rigidity, and bradykinesia
Spastic hyperreflexia, sustained ankle clonus, and Babinski sign
Aphasia, apraxia, and homonymous hemianopsia
questions.explain: Unlike basal ganglia disorders (resting tremor, hypertonia/rigidity, akinesia), cerebellar lesions produce action/intention tremor, hypotonia (pendular reflexes), and uncoordinated movement (ataxia, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia).

open.q: Define dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and intention tremor as seen in lateral cerebellar hemisphere lesions.
accept: Dysmetria: inaccurate range/distance judgment causing overshoot or undershoot of a target; Dysdiadochokinesia: impaired ability to execute rapid alternating movements; Intention tremor: coarse oscillatory tremor absent at rest that worsens as a limb nears its target
Target overshoot/undershoot (dysmetria), impaired rapid alternating movements (dysdiadochokinesia), terminal target-approaching tremor (intention tremor)

questions.sub: Basal Ganglia Anatomy and Direct vs Indirect Pathways
questions.q: Which nuclei constitute the 'striatum' (neostriatum) and the 'lentiform nucleus' of the basal ganglia?
options: Striatum = Caudate nucleus + Putamen; Lentiform nucleus = Putamen + Globus pallidus (internus and externus); functional basal ganglia circuitry also includes the Subthalamic nucleus (STN) and Substantia nigra (pars compacta and pars reticulata)
Striatum = Thalamus + Hypothalamus; Lentiform nucleus = Amygdala + Hippocampus
Striatum = Dentate nucleus + Red nucleus
Lentiform nucleus = Pons + Medulla oblongata
questions.explain: The caudate and putamen share identical histology and developmental origin (separated by the anterior limb of the internal capsule) and serve as the major input hub of the basal ganglia.

open.q: State the anatomical components of: (1) the striatum and (2) the lentiform nucleus.
accept: 1) Striatum: caudate nucleus and putamen; 2) Lentiform nucleus: putamen and globus pallidus
Caudate + putamen (striatum); putamen + globus pallidus (lentiform nucleus)

questions.sub: Basal Ganglia Anatomy and Direct vs Indirect Pathways
questions.q: Trace the 'Direct Pathway' of the basal ganglia and explain its net effect on thalamocortical motor facilitation:
options: Cerebral cortex (glutamate, +) -> Striatum (D1 medium spiny neurons; GABA, -) -> Globus pallidus internus / Substantia nigra pars reticulata (GPi/SNr; GABA, -) -> Ventral anterior / Ventral lateral (VA/VL) thalamus (glutamate, +) -> Motor cortex; inhibiting the tonically inhibitory GPi DISINHIBITS the thalamus, facilitating desired voluntary movement
Cerebral cortex -> STN -> GPi -> inhibits the thalamus to halt all movement
Striatum directly excites alpha motor neurons in the spinal cord via acetylcholine
GPi releases dopamine to inhibit the cerebral cortex
questions.explain: Two inhibitory GABAergic synapses in series (Striatum -| GPi -| Thalamus) equal net excitation (disinhibition) of the thalamocortical motor loop!

open.q: Trace the sequence of structures, neurotransmitters, and net effect on movement of the basal ganglia Direct Pathway.
accept: Cortex (+ glutamate) -> Striatum (- GABA) -> GPi/SNr (- GABA) -> VA/VL Thalamus (+ glutamate) -> Motor cortex; net effect is disinhibition of the thalamus to facilitate voluntary movement
Cortex (+) -> Striatum (-) -> GPi/SNr (-) -> Thalamus (+) -> Cortex; facilitates movement

questions.sub: Basal Ganglia Anatomy and Direct vs Indirect Pathways
questions.q: Trace the 'Indirect Pathway' of the basal ganglia and explain its net effect on movement:
options: Cerebral cortex (+ glutamate) -> Striatum (D2 neurons; - GABA) -> Globus pallidus externus (GPe; - GABA) -> Subthalamic nucleus (STN; + glutamate) -> GPi/SNr (- GABA) -> VA/VL thalamus -> Motor cortex; net effect is EXCITATION of GPi/SNr, which INHIBITS the thalamus and suppresses unwanted competing movements
Striatum directly excites the VA/VL thalamus via serotonin
Subthalamic nucleus releases GABA to inhibit GPi
Indirect pathway increases thalamocortical excitation to initiate movement
questions.explain: Three inhibitory GABAergic steps plus one excitatory glutamatergic step (STN -> GPi) produce net inhibition of the thalamus, acting as a brake on unwanted motor programs.

open.q: Trace the sequence of nuclei and net motor effect of the basal ganglia Indirect Pathway.
accept: Cortex (+) -> Striatum (-) -> GPe (-) -> Subthalamic nucleus (+) -> GPi/SNr (-) -> VA/VL Thalamus -> Motor cortex; net effect is increased GPi inhibition of the thalamus, suppressing unwanted movement
Cortex (+) -> Striatum (-) -> GPe (-) -> STN (+) -> GPi/SNr (-) -> Thalamus; inhibits unwanted movement

questions.sub: Basal Ganglia Anatomy and Direct vs Indirect Pathways
questions.q: How does dopamine released by the Substantia Nigra Pars Compacta (SNc) onto the striatum simultaneously activate the Direct Pathway and suppress the Indirect Pathway?
options: SNc dopamine binds excitatory Gs-coupled D1 receptors on direct-pathway striatal neurons (stimulating the movement-facilitating direct loop) AND binds inhibitory Gi-coupled D2 receptors on indirect-pathway striatal neurons (inhibiting the movement-suppressing indirect loop)—so dopamine promotes movement through BOTH pathways
Dopamine inhibits both D1 and D2 receptors to paralyze the body
Dopamine excites D2 receptors and inhibits D1 receptors
SNc releases acetylcholine onto the cerebellar cortex
questions.explain: D1 = excitatory (Gs), D2 = inhibitory (Gi). Consequently, loss of SNc dopamine in Parkinson's disease simultaneously under-activates the direct pathway AND over-activates the indirect pathway, locking GPi in hyperactive inhibition of the thalamus (bradykinesia/akinesia).

open.q: Explain how substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) dopamine modulates D1 versus D2 striatal receptors and why degeneration of SNc neurons produces bradykinesia in Parkinson's disease.
accept: Dopamine excites Gs-coupled D1 receptors (activating the direct pathway) and inhibits Gi-coupled D2 receptors (suppressing the indirect pathway); loss of SNc dopamine under-activates the direct pathway and over-activates the indirect pathway, causing excessive GPi inhibition of the thalamus and bradykinesia
D1 excitation + D2 inhibition both promote movement; SNc loss reduces direct pathway and increases indirect pathway, over-inhibiting thalamus

questions.q: Match each classic basal ganglia movement disorder with its specific lesioned structure and hallmark clinical motor features:
options: Parkinson's disease: substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) degeneration -> resting 'pill-rolling' tremor (4-6 Hz), bradykinesia/akinesia, cogwheel/lead-pipe rigidity, postural instability, shuffling festinating gait; Huntington's disease: striatal (caudate/putamen) GABA/enkephalin neuron atrophy -> chorea, dementia, behavioral changes; Hemiballismus: contralateral subthalamic nucleus (STN) lacunar stroke -> sudden violent, wild flinging movements of contralateral limbs
Parkinson's disease: cerebellar vermis infarct -> scanning speech and intention tremor
Hemiballismus: ipsilateral dorsal column lesion -> loss of vibration sense
Huntington's disease: anterior horn cell degeneration -> flaccid fasciculations
questions.explain: Destroying the contralateral STN removes excitatory drive to GPi, disinhibiting the thalamus excessively and unleashing violent proximal flinging movements (hemiballismus).

open.q: State the anatomical lesion site and cardinal motor sign for: (1) Parkinson's disease, (2) Huntington's disease, and (3) Hemiballismus.
accept: 1) Parkinson's: substantia nigra pars compacta (bradykinesia, resting tremor, rigidity, postural instability); 2) Huntington's: striatum / caudate & putamen (chorea); 3) Hemiballismus: contralateral subthalamic nucleus (violent proximal limb flinging)
SNc (bradykinesia/resting tremor/rigidity), striatum (chorea), contralateral STN (violent flinging)

questions.q: How do 'resting tremor' (basal ganglia / Parkinsonian) and 'intention tremor' (cerebellar) differ clinically?
options: Resting tremor (4-6 Hz 'pill-rolling') is maximal at rest when the limb is supported and diminishes or disappears during purposeful voluntary movement; intention tremor is absent at rest and emerges/worsens as the limb approaches a visual target during voluntary movement
Resting tremor occurs only while lifting heavy weights; intention tremor occurs only during deep sleep
Both tremors are caused by lesions of the primary visual cortex
Intention tremor disappears completely when reaching for a cup
questions.explain: Asking a patient to touch the examiner's finger cleanly separates resting tremor (improves with action) from cerebellar intention tremor (crescendos near the target).

open.q: Contrast resting tremor and intention tremor in terms of when each appears and its anatomical localization.
accept: Resting tremor: occurs at rest and improves with voluntary action (basal ganglia / substantia nigra lesion); Intention tremor: absent at rest and worsens as a limb approaches a target during voluntary movement (cerebellar / dentate-superior peduncle lesion)
Present at rest/diminishes with action (basal ganglia) vs absent at rest/worsens approaching target (cerebellum)

questions.q: What is 'syringomyelia', and why does a central cervical spinal cord syrinx (C8-T1) produce a classic 'cape-like' bilateral loss of pain and temperature over the shoulders and arms with preserved touch and vibration?
options: Cystic cavitation of the central canal (often associated with Arnold-Chiari type I malformation) compresses decussating second-order spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure (producing bilateral C8-T1 dissociated pain/temperature loss) while sparing the dorsal columns; as it enlarges laterally, it damages ventral horn alpha motor neurons causing intrinsic hand muscle atrophy
It destroys the medullary pyramids and spares the anterior white commissure
It selectively destroys dorsal root ganglia in the lumbar spine
It causes pure loss of vibration in the feet with intact pain sensation
questions.explain: Because decussating spinothalamic axons cross right next to the central canal in the anterior white commissure, central canal expansion interrupts pain/temperature bilaterally at those segments ('suspended' cape-like sensory loss).

open.q: Explain the neuroanatomical reason a central cervical syrinx causes bilateral 'cape-like' loss of pain and temperature while sparing fine touch and vibration.
accept: The expanding central canal cyst damages second-order spinothalamic axons decussating in the anterior white commissure at cervical levels, while sparing the posteriorly located dorsal columns
Destruction of spinothalamic fibers crossing in the anterior white commissure with sparing of the dorsal columns

questions.q: Which spinal cord tracts degenerate in 'Subacute Combined Degeneration' caused by Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency?
options: Bilateral dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus -> loss of vibration, proprioception, sensory ataxia, positive Romberg sign) AND bilateral lateral corticospinal tracts (spastic paraparesis, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign), plus peripheral neuropathy
Anterior white commissure only
Isolated trochlear nerve nuclei
Olfactory bulbs and optic chiasm
questions.explain: Vitamin B12 is required for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase; its deficiency impairs myelin synthesis in the heavily myelinated dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts.

open.q: Name the two major spinal cord tracts affected in Vitamin B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration) and their corresponding clinical deficits.
accept: Dorsal columns (loss of vibration and proprioception / sensory ataxia) and lateral corticospinal tracts (spastic weakness, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign)
Dorsal columns (proprioception/vibration loss) and lateral corticospinal tracts (UMN spasticity/Babinski)

questions.q: What is 'Tabes Dorsalis' (tertiary neurosyphilis), and how does it alter gait, reflexes, and sensory testing?
options: Demyelination and degeneration of dorsal nerve roots and dorsal columns, causing loss of vibration and proprioception, severe sensory ataxia with a high-stepping 'stamping' gait, positive Romberg sign, lightning lancinating pains, absent lower-limb deep tendon reflexes (areflexia), and Argyll Robertson pupils
Pure upper motor neuron spasticity with 4+ patellar reflexes
Isolated loss of pain and temperature with intact proprioception
Resting pill-rolling tremor and bradykinesia
questions.explain: Because dorsal root entry zone degeneration interrupts the afferent limb of muscle stretch reflexes as well as dorsal column proprioception, patients lose both position sense and knee/ankle reflexes.

open.q: Which spinal structures degenerate in tabes dorsalis, and why are deep tendon reflexes absent rather than hyperactive?
accept: Dorsal roots and dorsal columns; degeneration of dorsal root sensory afferents (including Type Ia spindle afferents) interrupts the afferent limb of the stretch reflex arc, causing areflexia
Dorsal roots and dorsal columns; loss of incoming dorsal root afferents breaks the stretch reflex arc

questions.sub: Brainstem Anatomy, Cranial Nerve Nuclei, and Rule of 4s
questions.q: What is 'Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia' (INO), which brainstem tract is lesioned, and what eye movements are seen when a patient with a RIGHT MLF lesion attempts to look to the LEFT?
options: Lesion of the myelinated Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF, connecting contralateral CN VI abducens interneurons to ipsilateral CN III medial rectus subnucleus); on attempted leftward gaze, the RIGHT eye fails to adduct past the midline while the abducting LEFT eye exhibits horizontal monocular nystagmus, WITH preserved convergence (because convergence uses separate supraocular pathways)
The left eye fails to abduct and convergence is completely absent
Both eyes deviate upward permanently
Lesion of the optic chiasm causing bitemporal hemianopsia
questions.explain: Multiple sclerosis in young adults (often bilateral INO) and lacunar brainstem stroke in older adults are the two classic causes of MLF lesions.

open.q: Describe the eye movement abnormality seen during horizontal gaze and during convergence in a patient with a lesion of the right Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF).
accept: On attempted leftward gaze, the right eye fails to adduct and the abducting left eye shows nystagmus; convergence remains intact
Impaired adduction of the ipsilateral (right) eye on contralateral gaze, abducting nystagmus of the contralateral eye, and preserved convergence

questions.sub: Brainstem Anatomy, Cranial Nerve Nuclei, and Rule of 4s
questions.q: How do 'Weber syndrome' (ventral midbrain stroke) and 'Benedikt syndrome' (midbrain tegmental stroke) differ clinically?
options: Weber syndrome (paramedian midbrain cerebral peduncle + exiting CN III fibers) causes ipsilateral CN III palsy (eye 'down and out', ptosis, dilated pupil) + contralateral spastic hemiparesis; Benedikt syndrome (midbrain tegmentum hitting CN III + red nucleus/dentatorubrothalamic fibers) causes ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral ataxia/intention tremor/choreoathetosis
Weber syndrome causes ipsilateral facial droop and hearing loss
Benedikt syndrome causes pure visual agnosia
Both syndromes are caused by anterior cerebral artery occlusion
questions.explain: Both are ventral/tegmental midbrain syndromes producing ipsilateral oculomotor palsy, distinguished by whether the lesion hits the crus cerebri (contralateral hemiparesis = Weber) or red nucleus/cerebellar outflow (contralateral ataxia/tremor = Benedikt).

open.q: Contrast the contralateral motor signs of midbrain Weber syndrome versus Benedikt syndrome.
accept: Both feature ipsilateral CN III palsy; Weber syndrome causes contralateral spastic hemiparesis (cerebral peduncle/corticospinal tract), whereas Benedikt syndrome causes contralateral ataxia/tremor/chorea (red nucleus and superior cerebellar peduncle fibers)
Contralateral hemiparesis (Weber) vs contralateral ataxia/tremor (Benedikt)

questions.sub: Brainstem Anatomy, Cranial Nerve Nuclei, and Rule of 4s
questions.q: What is 'Parinaud syndrome' (dorsal midbrain / pretectal syndrome, e.g., from a pineal gland tumor compressing the superior colliculi and pretectal area)?
options: Paralysis of upward conjugate gaze, light-near pupillary dissociation (pupils constrict to accommodation/convergence but poorly to direct light), convergence-retraction nystagmus, and bilateral eyelid retraction (Collier's sign)
Ipsilateral tongue paralysis and contralateral hemiplegia
Loss of pain and temperature over the entire left half of the body
Pure sensorineural deafness and vertigo
questions.explain: Pinealomas or aqueductal stenosis compress the dorsal midbrain pretectal area and vertical gaze center (rostral interstitial MLF / posterior commissure), producing classic upward-gaze palsy.

open.q: List three hallmark neuro-ophthalmologic signs of dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome.
accept: Upward conjugate gaze palsy, pupillary light-near dissociation, convergence-retraction nystagmus, and eyelid retraction
Upward gaze paralysis, light-near dissociation, convergence-retraction nystagmus

questions.sub: Brainstem Anatomy, Cranial Nerve Nuclei, and Rule of 4s
questions.q: What is the brainstem 'Rule of 4s' (Gates' clinical localization rule) for vascular brainstem strokes?
options: 4 midline motor nuclei (CN III, IV, VI, XII) and 4 midline tracts (Motor corticospinal, Medial lemniscus, Medial longitudinal fasciculus, Motor nuclei/fascicles — all starting with 'M') supplied by paramedian branches; 4 lateral cranial nerves (CN V, VII, VIII, IX/X/XI) and 4 lateral tracts (Spinocerebellar, Spinothalamic, Sensory nucleus of V, Sympathetic tract — all starting with 'S') supplied by circumferential arteries (PICA, AICA, SCA)
4 cerebellar hemispheres and 4 spinal cords
All cranial nerves exit the midbrain at level C4
4 arteries supply the retina exclusively
questions.explain: Midline 'M' structures (Motor tract, Medial lemniscus, MLF, Motor nuclei III/IV/VI/XII) vs Lateral 'S' structures (Spinocerebellar, Spinothalamic, Sensory V, Sympathetic) rapidly localize any brainstem stroke.

open.q: State the four lateral brainstem tracts beginning with 'S' in the clinical Rule of 4s.
accept: Spinocerebellar tract, Spinothalamic tract, Sensory nucleus/tract of trigeminal nerve (CN V), and Sympathetic (hypothalamospinal) fibers
Spinocerebellar, spinothalamic, sensory trigeminal, sympathetic pathway

questions.q: What is the 'Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex' (VOR), which cerebellar lobe calibrates its gain, and how does it stabilize vision during head rotation?
options: When the head rotates rapidly to the right, right horizontal semicircular canal afferents excite the right vestibular nucleus -> contralateral left abducens (CN VI) nucleus (abducts left eye) and via the right MLF excite the right oculomotor (CN III) medial rectus subnucleus (adducts right eye), driving smooth conjugate eye movement to the LEFT at equal velocity; calibrated by the vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe)
Rotating the head to the right causes both eyes to rotate rapidly to the right
The VOR is mediated by the dorsal columns and primary somatosensory cortex
The VOR functions only when the eyes are tightly closed
questions.explain: The VOR keeps images stabilized on the fovea during head movement; cerebellar flocculonodular lesions impair VOR gain adaptation and cause gaze-evoked nystagmus.

open.q: Trace the excitatory neural pathway that moves both eyes to the left when the head turns rapidly to the right during the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR).
accept: Right horizontal semicircular canal -> right vestibular nucleus -> contralateral left abducens (CN VI) nucleus (left lateral rectus) AND via right MLF to right oculomotor (CN III) nucleus (right medial rectus)
Right vestibular nucleus -> left CN VI (left abduction) + right MLF -> right CN III (right adduction)

questions.sub: Cerebellar Peduncles and Clinical Cerebellar Signs
questions.q: Why does alcohol intoxication cause acute slurred speech (dysarthria), wide-based staggering gait (truncal ataxia), nystagmus, and failed finger-to-nose testing?
options: Ethanol potentiates GABA-A receptor inhibition and suppresses glutamate signaling on cerebellar Purkinje and granule cells, acutely impairing both the spinocerebellum (vermis -> truncal/gait ataxia) and cerebrocerebellum (hemispheres -> limb dysmetria and dysarthria)
Ethanol selectively destroys the optic chiasm
Ethanol blocks acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction
Ethanol overstimulates the substantia nigra pars compacta
questions.explain: Chronic alcoholism additionally causes anterior cerebellar vermis degeneration (thiamine deficiency / direct toxicity), producing persistent wide-based gait ataxia even when sober.

open.q: Which part of the cerebellum is preferentially damaged in chronic alcoholism, and what specific gait abnormality results?
accept: Anterior cerebellar vermis; wide-based, staggering truncal/gait ataxia
Anterior vermis; wide-based gait/truncal ataxia

questions.sub: Basal Ganglia Anatomy and Direct vs Indirect Pathways
questions.q: What is the 'hyperdirect pathway' of the basal ganglia, and what functional role does it play in motor control?
options: Fast monosynaptic glutamatergic projections directly from frontal motor cortex to the subthalamic nucleus (STN -> GPi -> thalamus), rapidly halting or braking ongoing or premature motor programs before the direct pathway executes the selected action
A slow pathway from the spinal cord to the hippocampus
A direct projection from GPi to skeletal muscle
A pathway that releases serotonin onto the retina
questions.explain: Together, the hyperdirect (global brake), indirect (surround suppression), and direct (center facilitation) pathways act like a 'center-surround' selector for voluntary movement.

open.q: Describe the anatomical connection and functional purpose of the basal ganglia hyperdirect pathway.
accept: Direct excitatory glutamatergic projection from frontal cortex to the subthalamic nucleus (STN), which excites GPi/SNr to rapidly brake or suppress premature/ongoing movements
Cortex -> STN -> GPi/SNr; provides rapid global motor braking/inhibition

questions.q: Why are cholinergic striatal interneurons overactive in Parkinson's disease, and why do centrally acting muscarinic antagonists (e.g., benztropine, trihexyphenidyl) reduce Parkinsonian resting tremor?
options: Normally, SNc dopamine inhibits tonically active striatal cholinergic (ACh) interneurons via D2 receptors; loss of dopamine disinhibits striatal ACh release, tipping the dopamine/ACh balance toward excessive indirect-pathway activity—so antimuscarinic drugs restore neurochemical balance and dampen tremor
Striatal interneurons release dopamine onto the diaphragm
Benztropine converts acetylcholine into levodopa
Parkinson's disease is caused by excess brain dopamine
questions.explain: In the striatum, dopamine and acetylcholine act antagonistically; restoring dopamine (levodopa, dopamine agonists) or blocking excess acetylcholine (benztropine) rebalances striatal output.

open.q: Explain the opposing functional relationship between dopamine and acetylcholine within the striatum in Parkinson's disease.
accept: Dopamine normally inhibits striatal cholinergic interneurons via D2 receptors; dopamine depletion causes relative cholinergic overactivity, which antimuscarinic drugs (benztropine) counteract to reduce tremor
Dopamine and acetylcholine act antagonistically in the striatum; dopamine loss leads to cholinergic excess

questions.sub: Spinal Cord Laminae and Blood Supply
questions.q: Match Rexed laminae of the spinal cord gray matter with their key functional nuclei:
options: Lamina II: substantia gelatinosa (pain/temperature modulation, enkephalin interneurons); Lamina VII: intermediolateral cell column (T1-L2 sympathetic preganglionic neurons) and Clarke's column (C8-L2 dorsal spinocerebellar origin); Lamina IX: alpha and gamma lower motor neurons in the ventral horn
Lamina II contains alpha motor neurons innervating the quadriceps
Lamina IX contains primary visual cortex photoreceptors
Clarke's column is located in the sacral S4 segment exclusively
questions.explain: Rexed laminae I-VI form the dorsal sensory horn, lamina VII forms the intermediate zone (autonomic IML and Clarke's column), and laminae VIII-IX form the ventral motor horn.

open.q: State the functional nuclei located in: (1) Rexed lamina II, (2) Rexed lamina VII (T1-L2), and (3) Rexed lamina IX.
accept: 1) Lamina II: substantia gelatinosa (nociceptive modulation); 2) Lamina VII: intermediolateral cell column (sympathetic preganglionic neurons) and Clarke's column; 3) Lamina IX: alpha and gamma lower motor neurons
Substantia gelatinosa (II), intermediolateral/Clarke's column (VII), alpha/gamma motor neurons (IX)

questions.sub: Brainstem Anatomy, Cranial Nerve Nuclei, and Rule of 4s
questions.q: Which brainstem nucleus serves as the primary visceral sensory relay for taste (CN VII, IX, X) in its rostral gustatory part and baroreceptor/chemoreceptor/cardiorespiratory afferents (CN IX, X) in its caudal cardiorespiratory part?
options: Nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) in the dorsal medulla
Nucleus ambiguus
Red nucleus
Inferior olivary nucleus
questions.explain: Mnemonic: 'Solitary tract = Sensory' (taste + baroreceptor/chemoreceptor visceral afferents), whereas 'Ambiguus = Motor' (swallowing, palatal elevation, phonation via CN IX, X, XI).

open.q: Distinguish the functional roles of the medullary Nucleus Tractus Solitarius (NTS) versus the Nucleus Ambiguus.
accept: Nucleus tractus solitarius: visceral sensory nucleus receiving taste (rostral) and baroreceptor/chemoreceptor/gut afferents (caudal) via CN VII, IX, X; Nucleus ambiguus: branchial motor nucleus innervating pharyngeal, laryngeal, and palatal muscles (swallowing and speech) via CN IX, X, XI
Visceral sensory taste & baroreceptor/chemoreceptor relay (NTS) vs motor swallowing/speech (nucleus ambiguus)

questions.q: Where is the 'arbor vitae' located, and what is the histological organization of the three layers of the cerebellar cortex from superficial to deep?
options: Arbor vitae is the branching white matter tree inside the cerebellum; the three cortical layers from superficial to deep are: 1) Molecular layer (parallel fibers, stellate and basket inhibitory interneurons, Purkinje dendrites); 2) Purkinje cell layer (single monolayer of large flask-shaped Purkinje somata); 3) Granular layer (densely packed excitatory granule cells, mossy fiber rosettes, and Golgi cells)
Arbor vitae is in the cerebral frontal lobe; cerebellar cortex has six layers like neocortex
Purkinje cells are located in the deep white matter
Granular layer is the outermost pial layer
questions.explain: Unlike the 6-layered cerebral neocortex, the entire cerebellar cortex has a uniform 3-layered architecture (Molecular, Purkinje, Granular).

open.q: List the three histological layers of the cerebellar cortex from outermost (pial) to innermost (white matter).
accept: 1) Molecular layer, 2) Purkinje cell layer, 3) Granular layer
Molecular, Purkinje, Granular

questions.q: What is the genetic and neurochemical basis of Huntington's disease, and why do choreiform (dance-like) involuntary movements occur early in the disease?
options: Autosomal dominant CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion (>36-40 repeats, showing genetic anticipation) in the huntingtin (HTT) gene on chromosome 4p; preferential early degeneration of striatal GABA/enkephalin neurons of the INDIRECT pathway reduces GPi inhibition of the thalamus, unleashing excessive, involuntary dance-like movements (chorea)
X-linked deficiency of dystrophin causing muscle necrosis
Excessive dopamine secretion from the cerebellum
Autoimmune destruction of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
questions.explain: Early selective loss of indirect-pathway D2 striatal neurons removes the movement-suppressing brake (releasing chorea), whereas later loss of direct-pathway neurons leads to akinetic-rigid end-stage disease.

open.q: Explain why early selective degeneration of striatal indirect-pathway neurons in Huntington's disease produces choreiform involuntary movements.
accept: Loss of indirect-pathway striatal neurons reduces inhibition of GPe, increasing GPe inhibition of the subthalamic nucleus (STN), which decreases GPi excitation and disinhibits the thalamus—producing excessive involuntary movements (chorea)
Loss of the movement-suppressing indirect pathway leads to excessive thalamocortical excitation and chorea

questions.q: At what vertebral level does the adult human spinal cord terminate as the conus medullaris, and what clinical syndrome results from compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots below L1-L2?
options: Terminates at the L1-L2 intervertebral disc in adults (L3 in newborns); compression of the lumbosacral roots below L1-L2 produces 'Cauda Equina Syndrome'—characterized by severe radicular pain, asymmetric flaccid LMN leg weakness, areflexia, saddle anesthesia (S2-S4), and early urinary/fecal incontinence
Terminates at S5; compression produces pure upper motor neuron spasticity
Terminates at C7; compression causes blindness
Terminates at T4; compression causes decerebrate rigidity
questions.explain: Because the conus medullaris ends at L1-L2, lumbar punctures are safely performed at L3-L4 or L4-L5, and large central L4-L5 disc herniations compress peripheral cauda equina roots (LMN deficit) rather than spinal cord parenchyma.

open.q: State the adult vertebral termination level of the spinal cord and list four hallmark clinical features of Cauda Equina Syndrome.
accept: L1-L2 vertebral level; asymmetric LMN flaccid leg weakness, absent knee/ankle reflexes, saddle anesthesia (perineal sensory loss), severe radicular pain, and bladder/bowel sphincter dysfunction
L1-L2; saddle anesthesia, asymmetric flaccid leg weakness, areflexia, urinary/bowel incontinence

questions.sub: Brainstem Anatomy, Cranial Nerve Nuclei, and Rule of 4s
questions.q: What is 'central pontine myelinolysis' (osmotic demyelination syndrome), how is it precipitated, and what neurological picture does it produce?
options: Acute demyelination of the basis pontis caused by overly rapid intravenous correction of severe chronic hyponatremia (>8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours), destroying corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers and producing acute quadriparesis, dysarthria, dysphagia, and Locked-In Syndrome
Slow peripheral neuropathy caused by mild hyperkalemia
Cerebellar hemorrhage caused by hypotension
Optic neuritis caused by vitamin A excess
questions.explain: Brain cells chronically adapted to hyponatremia have extruded organic osmolytes; rapid serum Na+ elevation draws water out of oligodendrocytes in the tightly packed basis pontis, causing osmotic myelinolysis.

open.q: What electrolyte correction error precipitates osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis), and what motor syndrome does it cause?
accept: Overly rapid correction of severe chronic hyponatremia; causes acute quadriparesis, bulbar palsy (dysarthria/dysphagia), and Locked-In Syndrome
Rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia; quadriparesis and Locked-In Syndrome

questions.q: A 67-year-old man with atrial fibrillation suddenly develops severe vertigo, nausea, vomiting, hiccups, hoarseness, dysphagia, loss of pain and temperature over the LEFT side of his face and RIGHT side of his trunk and limbs, left-sided limb ataxia, and a left-sided ptosis and miosis (Horner syndrome). Strength in all four limbs is 5/5. Which artery is occluded?
options: Left vertebral artery or Left Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA) — causing Left Lateral Medullary (Wallenberg) Syndrome
Right Middle Cerebral Artery
Left Anterior Spinal Artery
Right Posterior Cerebral Artery
questions.explain: Crossed sensory loss (ipsilateral left face via spinal V nucleus + contralateral right body via spinothalamic tract), dysphagia/hoarseness (left nucleus ambiguus), ipsilateral ataxia (inferior cerebellar peduncle), and left Horner syndrome with preserved motor strength (spared medial pyramid) are pathognomonic for Left Wallenberg syndrome.

open.q: Localize the lesion and occluded artery in a patient with hoarseness, dysphagia, left facial pain/temperature loss, right body pain/temperature loss, left ataxia, and left Horner syndrome.
accept: Left lateral medulla oblongata; occlusion of the left vertebral artery or left Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA) (Wallenberg syndrome)
Left lateral medulla / left PICA or vertebral artery

questions.q: A 71-year-old man develops sudden left-sided spastic hemiparesis, loss of vibration and joint position sense in his left arm and leg, and deviation of his protruded tongue to the RIGHT (with right-sided tongue atrophy and fasciculations). Where is the lesion?
options: Right medial medulla oblongata (paramedian branches of the right vertebral or anterior spinal artery — Medial Medullary Syndrome)
Left lateral pons
Right cerebellar hemisphere
Left cerebral motor cortex
questions.explain: LMN damage to the right hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) weakens the right genioglossus muscle, so the intact left genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the paralyzed RIGHT side, while right medullary pyramid and medial lemniscus lesions cause contralateral LEFT hemiparesis and dorsal column loss.

open.q: Identify the anatomical lesion in a patient with right-sided tongue deviation on protrusion, left hemiparesis, and left loss of vibration/proprioception.
accept: Right medial medulla oblongata (Medial Medullary / Dejerine syndrome)
Right medial medulla

questions.q: A 68-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of progressive slowness of movement (bradykinesia), difficulty initiating walking with short shuffling steps and absent arm swing, stooped posture, expressionless 'masked' face, cogwheel rigidity at the wrists, and a 5 Hz 'pill-rolling' tremor of his right hand that disappears when he reaches for a glass of water. What histological finding is present in his substantia nigra pars compacta?
options: Loss of pigmented dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta with intracytoplasmic eosinophilic alpha-synuclein inclusions (Lewy bodies)
Neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau in the hippocampus only
Demyelinating plaques in the medial longitudinal fasciculus
Negri bodies in cerebellar Purkinje cells
questions.explain: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease is characterized by depigmentation of the neuromelanin-rich substantia nigra pars compacta and alpha-synuclein-positive Lewy bodies.

open.q: Name the degenerating brainstem structure and characteristic intraneuronal protein inclusion in idiopathic Parkinson's disease.
accept: Substantia nigra pars compacta (dopaminergic neurons); Lewy bodies (composed of alpha-synuclein)
Substantia nigra pars compacta; alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies

questions.q: A 74-year-old hypertensive man suddenly develops wild, violent, uncontrollable flinging movements of his right arm and right leg ('hemiballismus') that persist continuously while awake and subside only during sleep. MRI reveals a small acute lacunar infarction. Which specific nucleus is infarcted?
options: Left subthalamic nucleus (STN)
Right subthalamic nucleus (STN)
Right cerebellar dentate nucleus
Left nucleus tractus solitarius
questions.explain: A lacunar stroke in the contralateral (LEFT) subthalamic nucleus removes excitatory glutamatergic drive to left GPi, disinhibiting the left VA/VL thalamus and left motor cortex, which drives wild involuntary movements of the RIGHT limbs.

open.q: Which specific basal ganglia nucleus and side are infarcted in a patient who suddenly develops acute right-sided hemiballismus?
accept: Left (contralateral) subthalamic nucleus
Left subthalamic nucleus

questions.q: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for frequent falls and progressive difficulty walking over 6 months. Examination shows a wide-based, unsteady truncal gait, inability to walk tandem (heel-to-toe), and nystagmus, while individual finger-to-nose coordination when lying down is relatively preserved. MRI shows a midline cerebellar tumor arising from the roof of the fourth ventricle (medulloblastoma). Which functional zone of the cerebellum is compressed?
options: Midline cerebellar vermis and flocculonodular lobe (spinocerebellum / vestibulocerebellum)
Left lateral cerebrocerebellar hemisphere only
Left internal capsule
Right putamen
questions.explain: Midline cerebellar lesions (vermis and flocculonodular lobe, classic for childhood medulloblastoma) cause truncal/gait ataxia and nystagmus, whereas lateral hemispheric lesions (classic for pilocytic astrocytoma) cause ipsilateral limb appendicular ataxia.

open.q: Contrast the clinical presentation of a midline cerebellar vermis/flocculonodular lesion versus a lateral cerebellar hemisphere lesion.
accept: Midline vermis/flocculonodular lesion: truncal and gait ataxia (wide-based unsteady stance) and nystagmus; Lateral cerebellar hemisphere lesion: ipsilateral appendicular limb ataxia (dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia)
Truncal/gait ataxia & nystagmus (midline vermis) vs ipsilateral limb ataxia/intention tremor (lateral hemisphere)

questions.q: A 65-year-old man undergoes surgical repair of a descending thoracic aortic aneurysm and awakens postoperatively with flaccid paraplegia (later evolving to spastic paraplegia), urinary retention, and bilateral loss of pain and temperature below the T10 dermatome, while vibration and joint position sense in his toes remain completely intact. Which vessel was compromised?
options: Great radicular artery of Adamkiewicz supplying the Anterior Spinal Artery (Anterior Spinal Artery syndrome)
Bilateral posterior spinal arteries
Right middle cerebral artery
Basilar artery apex
questions.explain: The artery of Adamkiewicz (usually arising from a left posterior intercostal artery between T8 and L2) provides the dominant blood supply to the lower anterior spinal artery; ischemia spares the dorsal columns supplied by the paired posterior spinal arteries.

open.q: Identify the artery whose occlusion during thoracic aortic surgery causes bilateral lower-limb paralysis and loss of pain/temperature be_low T10 with spared vibration and proprioception.
accept: Great radicular artery of Adamkiewicz / Anterior spinal artery
Artery of Adamkiewicz (anterior spinal artery)

questions.q: A 34-year-old woman presents with progressive weakness and wasting of the small intrinsic muscles of both hands ('claw hand') and loss of pain and temperature sensation over both shoulders, upper chest, and arms in a 'cape-like' distribution, while light touch and vibration in her hands are normal. Cervical spine MRI shows an Arnold-Chiari type I malformation with a fluid-filled cavity expanding inside the C6-T1 spinal cord. What is the diagnosis?
options: Syringomyelia
Tabes dorsalis
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Subacute combined degeneration
questions.explain: A central cervical syrinx interrupts crossing spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure (cape-like pain/temp loss) and then extends into the C8-T1 ventral horns (bilateral intrinsic hand LMN atrophy).

open.q: What diagnosis is indicated by bilateral cape-like loss of pain and temperature, preserved vibration/proprioception, and intrinsic hand muscle atrophy in a patient with a Chiari I malformation?
accept: Syringomyelia
Cervical syringomyelia

questions.q: A 29-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis complains of double vision when looking to the right. On horizontal gaze to the right, her LEFT eye fails to adduct across the midline and her abducting RIGHT eye shows horizontal nystagmus; however, when she focuses on a finger moving toward her nose, both eyes converge normally. Which tract is demyelinated?
options: Left Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF) — Left Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO)
Right optic nerve (CN II)
Left trochlear nerve (CN IV)
Right abducens nerve (CN VI)
questions.explain: An INO is named for the side of the adducting eye (left eye fails to adduct on rightward gaze = left MLF lesion); preserved convergence rules out a medial rectus muscle or CN III nuclear lesion.

open.q: Name the lesioned tract and side in a patient whose left eye fails to adduct on rightward gaze, whose right eye shows abducting nystagmus, and whose convergence is intact.
accept: Left Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF) (Left internuclear ophthalmoplegia)
Left MLF

questions.q: A 55-year-old man with severe chronic hyponatremia (serum Na+ 106 mEq/L) has his sodium corrected rapidly to 132 mEq/L over 18 hours. Three days later, he develops acute flaccid then spastic quadriplegia and complete loss of speech and facial movement, yet remains fully alert and answers yes/no questions accurately using vertical eye movements and blinking. What condition has developed?
options: Osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis) producing Locked-In Syndrome
Brain death
Vegetative state with cortical necrosis
Guillain-Barre peripheral neuropathy
questions.explain: Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia causes osmotic demyelination of the basis pontis, sparing the dorsal tegmental ARAS and vertical gaze pathways.

open.q: Name the pathological process and resulting clinical syndrome when rapid sodium correction causes quadriparesis, mutism, and preserved consciousness with vertical eye-movement communication.
accept: Osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis) causing Locked-In Syndrome
Central pontine myelinolysis / Locked-In Syndrome

questions.q: A 62-year-old man with uncontrolled hypertension experiences sudden-onset left-sided ptosis, a dilated unreactive left pupil (6 mm), deviation of the left eye 'down and out,' and spastic paralysis of his right arm and right leg. Where is the stroke located?
options: Left ventral midbrain involving exiting oculomotor (CN III) nerve fascicles and the left cerebral peduncle (Weber syndrome)
Right caudal pons
Left lateral medulla
Right cerebellar hemisphere
questions.explain: Ipsilateral CN III palsy (including parasympathetic pupillomotor fibers -> mydriasis, plus unopposed lateral rectus CN VI and superior oblique CN IV -> 'down and out') + contralateral hemiparesis localizes to the ventral midbrain (Weber syndrome).

open.q: Localize the lesion in a patient presenting with left oculomotor nerve palsy (ptosis, mydriasis, eye 'down and out') and right-sided hemiparesis.
accept: Left ventral midbrain (Weber syndrome — involving left CN III fascicles and left cerebral peduncle / corticospinal tract)
Left ventral midbrain (Weber syndrome)

questions.q: How are fibers somatotopically organized within the dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis vs fasciculus cuneatus) and within the lateral spinothalamic tract?
options: In the dorsal columns, sacral/lower-limb fibers lie MEDIALLY (fasciculus gracilis) and cervical/upper-limb fibers are added LATERALLY (fasciculus cuneatus); in the lateral spinothalamic tract, cervical fibers lie MEDIALLY and sacral/lower-limb fibers lie LATERALLY (closest to the outer surface)
Sacral fibers lie laterally in the dorsal columns and medially in the spinothalamic tract
All spinal tracts are randomly mixed with zero somatotopic map
Cervical fibers travel in the cauda equina
questions.explain: Because sacral spinothalamic fibers sit superficially on the lateral periphery of the cord, an extramedullary tumor compressing the cord from the outside affects sacral/leg pain and temperature FIRST ('sacral loss'), whereas an intramedullary central tumor spares sacral fibers until late ('sacral sparing').

open.q: State the medial-to-lateral somatotopic order of cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and sacral fibers in: (1) the dorsal columns and (2) the lateral spinothalamic tract.
accept: 1) Dorsal columns: Sacral -> Lumbar -> Thoracic -> Cervical from medial to lateral; 2) Lateral spinothalamic tract: Cervical -> Thoracic -> Lumbar -> Sacral from medial to lateral
Dorsal columns: S-L-T-C (medial to lateral); Spinothalamic: C-T-L-S (medial to lateral)

questions.q: Why does an intramedullary spinal cord tumor (growing outward from the central gray matter) classically exhibit 'sacral sparing' of pain and temperature sensation?
options: In the lateral spinothalamic tract, cervical and thoracic fibers lie medially (nearest the expanding central tumor) while sacral fibers lie most laterally near the pial surface and are compressed last
Sacral spinothalamic fibers travel through the vagus nerve
The sacral spinal cord has no pain receptors
Intramedullary tumors compress the dorsal columns exclusively
questions.explain: Sacral sparing (preserved perianal/S3-S5 pain and temperature sensation) is a classic clinical sign distinguishing intramedullary lesions from extramedullary cord compression.

open.q: Explain the anatomical basis of 'sacral sparing' in intramedullary spinal cord lesions.
accept: In the lateral spinothalamic tract, sacral fibers are laminated most laterally near the outer surface of the cord, so an expanding central intramedullary lesion damages medial cervical/thoracic fibers first and spares sacral sensation until late
Sacral spinothalamic axons sit most laterally and are compressed last by an expanding central cord lesion

questions.q: How are lower motor neurons in the spinal ventral horn (Lamina IX) somatotopically arranged from medial to lateral and from anterior to posterior?
options: Medial motor nuclei innervate AXIAL and proximal trunk muscles, whereas lateral motor nuclei innervate DISTAL limb muscles (hands/feet); anterior motor neurons innervate EXTENSORS, whereas posterior motor neurons innervate FLEXORS
Lateral motor nuclei innervate the diaphragm; medial motor nuclei innervate the fingers
Posterior ventral horn neurons innervate extensors; anterior innervate flexors
There is no somatotopic organization in the ventral horn
questions.explain: Medial = axial/trunk, Lateral = distal limbs; Anterior = extensors, Posterior = flexors.

open.q: State the somatotopic organization of ventral horn lower motor neurons (medial vs lateral, and anterior vs posterior).
accept: Medial: axial/proximal trunk muscles; Lateral: distal limb muscles; Anterior: extensor muscles; Posterior: flexor muscles
Medial = axial, Lateral = distal; Anterior = extensors, Posterior = flexors

questions.sub: Brainstem Anatomy, Cranial Nerve Nuclei, and Rule of 4s
questions.q: Which cranial nerves carry preganglionic PARASYMPATHETIC efferent fibers from brainstem nuclei, and what are their respective nuclei and target ganglia?
options: CN III (Edinger-Westphal nucleus -> ciliary ganglion -> sphincter pupillae & ciliary muscle); CN VII (superior salivatory nucleus -> pterygopalatine & submandibular ganglia -> lacrimal, submandibular, sublingual glands); CN IX (inferior salivatory nucleus -> otic ganglion -> parotid gland); CN X (dorsal motor nucleus of vagus & nucleus ambiguus -> intramural ganglia of thoracic & abdominal viscera)
CN I, CN II, CN IV, and CN XII carry all parasympathetic fibers
CN V, CN VI, and CN VIII supply parasympathetic innervation to the heart
All brainstem parasympathetic fibers arise from the red nucleus
questions.explain: Craniosacral parasympathetic outflow consists of cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X plus sacral spinal segments S2-S4.

open.q: List the four cranial nerves that carry parasympathetic preganglionic fibers along with their brainstem nuclei of origin.
accept: CN III (Edinger-Westphal nucleus), CN VII (superior salivatory nucleus), CN IX (inferior salivatory nucleus), and CN X (dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus / nucleus ambiguus)
CN III (Edinger-Westphal), CN VII (superior salivatory), CN IX (inferior salivatory), CN X (dorsal motor nucleus)

questions.sub: Brainstem Anatomy, Cranial Nerve Nuclei, and Rule of 4s
questions.q: Why does an upper motor neuron (corticobulbar) lesion cause paralysis of ONLY the contralateral LOWER half of the face (sparing the forehead), whereas a lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve (CN VII, e.g., Bell's palsy) paralyzes BOTH the upper and lower halves of the ipsilateral face?
options: The dorsal subnucleus of the facial motor nucleus (innervating the upper face/forehead frontalis and orbicularis oculi) receives BILATERAL corticobulbar innervation from both cerebral hemispheres, whereas the ventral subnucleus (innervating the lower face) receives ONLY CONTRALATERAL corticobulbar input
The forehead is innervated by the trigeminal nerve (CN V)
The lower face receives bilateral corticobulbar input while the forehead receives ipsilateral input
Bell's palsy affects the primary motor cortex
questions.explain: Similarly, corticobulbar innervation to the hypoglossal nucleus (genioglossus) is predominantly contralateral, while nucleus ambiguus and trigeminal motor nuclei receive bilateral corticobulbar input.

open.q: Explain the corticobulbar innervation pattern of the facial motor nucleus (CN VII) that explains forehead sparing in a unilateral stroke.
accept: Upper facial muscles (forehead) receive bilateral corticobulbar projections from both motor cortices, whereas lower facial muscles receive exclusively contralateral corticobulbar innervation
Bilateral corticobulbar input to upper face vs contralateral-only input to lower face

questions.sub: Brainstem Anatomy, Cranial Nerve Nuclei, and Rule of 4s
questions.q: What are the clinical features of 'Lateral Pontine Syndrome' (Anterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery / AICA stroke) that distinguish it from Lateral Medullary (PICA) Syndrome?
options: Ipsilateral facial paralysis (CN VII nucleus/fascicles), ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus (cochlear nuclei/internal auditory artery), and loss of corneal blink reflex, in addition to crossed pain/temperature loss, vertigo, ipsilateral ataxia, and Horner syndrome
Ipsilateral tongue deviation and contralateral hemiplegia
Isolated downward and outward eye deviation
Bilateral lower extremity paraplegia
questions.explain: Mnemonic: 'Facial droop means AICA's pooped' (CN VII & VIII in lateral pons), whereas 'Hoarseness and dysphagia mean PICA' (nucleus ambiguus CN IX/X in lateral medulla).

open.q: Which cranial nerve deficits distinguish Lateral Pontine (AICA) syndrome from Lateral Medullary (PICA) syndrome?
accept: Lateral pontine (AICA) syndrome causes ipsilateral facial paralysis (CN VII) and sensorineural deafness/tinnitus (CN VIII), whereas lateral medullary (PICA) syndrome causes dysphagia and hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus CN IX/X)
Facial palsy (CN VII) and deafness (CN VIII) in AICA vs dysphagia/hoarseness (CN IX/X) in PICA

questions.sub: Brainstem Anatomy, Cranial Nerve Nuclei, and Rule of 4s
questions.q: Which structure in the dorsal pons serves as the horizontal gaze center coordinating conjugate lateral eye movements?
options: Paramedian Pontine Reticular Formation (PPRF), which projects to the ipsilateral abducens (CN VI) nucleus (abducting the ipsilateral eye) and via the contralateral Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF) to the contralateral oculomotor (CN III) medial rectus subnucleus (adducting the contralateral eye)
Superior colliculus
Inferior olivary nucleus
Substantia nigra pars reticulata
questions.explain: A destructive lesion of the right PPRF or right CN VI nucleus causes inability to look to the right (conjugate gaze palsy to the side of the lesion), whereas a destructive right frontal eye field lesion causes gaze deviation toward the right (inability to look away from the lesion).

open.q: Trace the pathway from the right Paramedian Pontine Reticular Formation (PPRF) that produces conjugate horizontal gaze to the right.
accept: Right PPRF excites right abducens (CN VI) nucleus (right lateral rectus abduction) AND abducens interneurons cross to ascend in the left MLF to excite the left oculomotor (CN III) medial rectus subnucleus (left eye adduction)
Right PPRF -> right CN VI nucleus (right abduction) + left MLF -> left CN III nucleus (left adduction)

questions.sub: Reticular Formation, ARAS, and Decorticate vs Decerebrate Posturing
questions.q: Which brainstem reticular/tegmental nuclei synthesize the major monoamine neurotransmitters—norepinephrine, serotonin (5-HT), and dopamine—projecting widely across the CNS?
options: Norepinephrine: Locus coeruleus (dorsal pons); Serotonin (5-HT): Raphe nuclei (midline brainstem); Dopamine: Substantia nigra pars compacta (nigrostriatal) and Ventral tegmental area (mesolimbic/mesocortical)
Norepinephrine: Dentate nucleus; Serotonin: Optic chiasm; Dopamine: Pineal gland
All three monoamines are synthesized exclusively in the spinal dorsal horn
Serotonin is synthesized in the locus coeruleus and dopamine in the raphe nuclei
questions.explain: Locus coeruleus (arousal, attention, stress/panic), Raphe nuclei (mood, sleep-wake regulation, descending analgesia), and VTA/SNc (reward, cognition, motor control) form the core neuromodulatory systems of the brainstem.

open.q: Match each monoamine neurotransmitter with its primary brainstem nucleus of origin: (1) Norepinephrine, (2) Serotonin, and (3) Dopamine.
accept: 1) Norepinephrine: locus coeruleus; 2) Serotonin: raphe nuclei; 3) Dopamine: substantia nigra pars compacta and ventral tegmental area (VTA)
Locus coeruleus (NE), raphe nuclei (5-HT), SNc & VTA (DA)
