questions.sub: Cerebellar Microcircuitry: Purkinje, Granule, Climbing, and Mossy Fibers
questions.q: How do 'basket cells' and 'stellate cells' in the cerebellar molecular layer shape Purkinje cell activity?
options: Excited by granule cell parallel fibers, basket and stellate cells release GABA onto adjacent off-beam Purkinje cells (basket cells form dense inhibitory pericellular baskets around Purkinje somata/axon hillocks), creating lateral inhibition that focuses active Purkinje cell beams
They release glutamate to excite Purkinje cells directly
They myelinate spinal motor axons
They secrete cerebrospinal fluid into the cisterna magna
questions.explain: Parallel fibers excite an on-beam row of Purkinje cells while simultaneously exciting basket and stellate interneurons that inhibit flanking off-beam Purkinje cells—a cerebellar form of spatial lateral inhibition.

open.q: What neurotransmitter do cerebellar basket and stellate cells release, and how do they sharpen cerebellar cortical output?
accept: GABA (inhibitory); excited by parallel fibers, they inhibit flanking off-beam Purkinje cells (lateral inhibition) to focus cerebellar output
GABA; lateral inhibition of adjacent Purkinje cells

questions.q: What is the 'comparator function' of the spinocerebellum during an ongoing voluntary limb movement?
options: It receives BOTH an 'efference copy' (internal copy of the intended motor command from motor cortex via pontine nuclei) AND real-time proprioceptive feedback from the moving limb (via spinocerebellar tracts), computing error signals and sending corrective signals via interposed/fastigial nuclei to smooth movement and stop it accurately at the target
It compares arterial PO2 with venous PCO2
It stores long-term declarative episodic memories
It regulates renal sodium reabsorption
questions.explain: When this comparator loop fails in cerebellar disease, the limb overshoots or undershoots the target (dysmetria) and oscillates back and forth as visual feedback tries to correct it (intention tremor).

open.q: Explain the two inputs compared by the spinocerebellum during voluntary movement to prevent overshoot (dysmetria).
accept: Intended motor plan ('efference copy' from motor cortex via pontine nuclei) and actual limb position/velocity feedback (from spinocerebellar proprioceptive tracts)
Cortical motor command copy and spinocerebellar proprioceptive feedback

questions.q: Why is oral L-DOPA (levodopa) co-administered with carbidopa in the treatment of Parkinson's disease rather than giving dopamine directly?
options: Dopamine is hydrophilic and cannot cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB); lipid-soluble L-DOPA crosses the BBB via the large neutral amino acid transporter and is converted to dopamine by central DOPA decarboxylase, while carbidopa inhibits peripheral DOPA decarboxylase outside the BBB (preventing peripheral nausea/arrhythmias and increasing CNS L-DOPA bioavailability)
Carbidopa crosses the BBB and destroys the subthalamic nucleus
Dopamine crosses the BBB instantly but is degraded by pepsin in the stomach
L-DOPA blocks D2 receptors in the striatum
questions.explain: Carbidopa cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, so it selectively blocks peripheral conversion of L-DOPA to dopamine in the gut and vasculature without inhibiting dopamine synthesis inside the brain.

open.q: Explain why L-DOPA is used instead of dopamine for Parkinson's disease and why carbidopa is combined with it.
accept: Dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier whereas L-DOPA can; carbidopa inhibits peripheral DOPA decarboxylase without crossing the BBB, reducing peripheral side effects and increasing the fraction of L-DOPA entering the brain
L-DOPA crosses the BBB while dopamine cannot; carbidopa blocks peripheral decarboxylation to boost brain delivery and prevent nausea/hypotension

questions.q: How does Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) of the subthalamic nucleus (STN) or globus pallidus internus (GPi) relieve motor symptoms in advanced Parkinson's disease?
options: High-frequency electrical stimulation (~130 Hz) overrides and suppresses abnormal, hyperactive oscillatory burst firing in the STN or GPi, releasing the VA/VL thalamus from excessive GABAergic inhibition and restoring smoother thalamocortical motor drive
DBS destroys the primary motor cortex
DBS stimulates insulin secretion from the pancreas
DBS increases GABA release from GPi onto the thalamus by 500%
questions.explain: In Parkinson's disease, loss of SNc dopamine causes pathological hyperactivity of the STN and GPi; high-frequency DBS functionally dampens STN/GPi output.

open.q: Name the two primary basal ganglia targets for Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) in Parkinson's disease and explain why suppressing their overactivity improves movement.
accept: Subthalamic nucleus (STN) and globus pallidus internus (GPi); suppressing their pathological overactivity reduces excessive GABAergic inhibition of the VA/VL thalamus, restoring thalamocortical motor facilitation
STN and GPi; reduces excessive inhibition of the motor thalamus

questions.sub: Spinal Cord Laminae and Blood Supply
questions.q: How do 'conus medullaris syndrome' (lesion at L1-L2) and 'cauda equina syndrome' (lesion of nerve roots below L2) differ clinically?
options: Conus medullaris syndrome presents with sudden, symmetric saddle anesthesia, early severe bladder/bowel incontinence and impotence, minimal leg weakness, and mixed UMN/LMN signs; Cauda equina syndrome presents with gradual, asymmetric severe radicular leg pain, asymmetric flaccid LMN leg weakness/areflexia, asymmetric saddle anesthesia, and late sphincter dysfunction
Conus medullaris syndrome causes isolated facial droop
Cauda equina syndrome causes 4+ hyperreflexia and bilateral Babinski signs
Both syndromes present identically with pure aphasia
questions.explain: Conus medullaris is central spinal cord tissue (symmetric sacral autonomic/saddle deficits early), whereas cauda equina consists of peripheral nerve roots (asymmetric radicular pain and LMN leg weakness).

open.q: Contrast conus medullaris syndrome and cauda equina syndrome in terms of symmetry, radicular pain severity, and onset of sphincter dysfunction.
accept: Conus medullaris: symmetric deficits, mild/less prominent radicular pain, early severe bladder/bowel sphincter dysfunction; Cauda equina: asymmetric deficits, severe radicular pain, later bladder/bowel dysfunction
Symmetric/early sphincter loss/mild pain (conus) vs asymmetric/late sphincter loss/severe radicular pain (cauda equina)

questions.sub: Brainstem Anatomy, Cranial Nerve Nuclei, and Rule of 4s
questions.q: Which brainstem nucleus is responsible for the 'chemoreceptor trigger zone' (CTZ) inducing vomiting in response to blood-borne toxins, chemotherapeutic drugs, and uremia?
options: Area postrema, a circumventricular organ lacking a blood-brain barrier located on the dorsal surface of the caudal medulla at the inferior floor of the fourth ventricle
Superior colliculus in the dorsal midbrain
Inferior salivatory nucleus
Red nucleus
questions.explain: Because the area postrema has fenestrated capillaries outside the blood-brain barrier and rich dopamine D2, serotonin 5-HT3, and neurokinin NK1 receptors, emetogenic toxins trigger vomiting via projections to the medullary vomiting center.

open.q: Name the circumventricular organ in the caudal medulla that acts as the chemoreceptor trigger zone for vomiting and explain why blood-borne toxins reach it directly.
accept: Area postrema; it lacks a blood-brain barrier (has fenestrated capillaries), allowing circulating toxins and drugs to stimulate its receptors directly
Area postrema; lacks a blood-brain barrier

questions.sub: Brainstem Anatomy, Cranial Nerve Nuclei, and Rule of 4s
questions.q: Where do the cranial nerves emerge on the ventral surface of the brainstem?
options: CN I & II: forebrain; CN III: interpeduncular fossa of midbrain; CN IV: dorsal midbrain (only cranial nerve exiting dorsally, and decussates before exiting); CN V: mid-lateral pons; CN VI, VII, VIII: pontomedullary junction (medial to lateral); CN IX, X, XI: postolivary sulcus of medulla; CN XII: preolivary sulcus (between pyramid and olive)
All twelve cranial nerves exit through the foramen magnum
CN XII exits from the dorsal midbrain and CN IV exits from the preolivary sulcus
CN VI, VII, and VIII exit from the cerebral peduncles
questions.explain: Notice the landmarks around the medullary olive: CN XII exits medially in the preolivary sulcus (between pyramid and olive), whereas CN IX, X, and XI exit laterally in the postolivary (retro-olivary) sulcus.

open.q: Which cranial nerve exits the dorsal aspect of the brainstem, and which cranial nerves exit in the preolivary versus postolivary sulci of the medulla?
accept: Trochlear nerve (CN IV) exits dorsally; Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) exits the preolivary sulcus; Glossopharyngeal (CN IX), Vagus (CN X), and cranial Accessory (CN XI) exit the postolivary sulcus
CN IV (dorsal); CN XII (preolivary); CN IX, X, XI (postolivary)

questions.sub: Reticular Formation, ARAS, and Decorticate vs Decerebrate Posturing
questions.q: What is the 'corticospinal-reticulospinal control of micturition' mediated by the Pontine Micturition Center (Barrington's nucleus)?
options: Barrington's nucleus in the dorsal pons coordinates voiding by simultaneously exciting sacral (S2-S4) parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic neurons (contracting the detrusor muscle) and inhibiting lumbar sympathetic and Onuf's nucleus pudendal somatic motor neurons (relaxing internal and external urethral sphincters), under inhibitory control from the medial prefrontal cortex
The pontine micturition center paralyzes the detrusor muscle during urination
Micturition is controlled solely by the cerebellar flocculonodular lobe
Onuf's nucleus is located in the midbrain red nucleus
questions.explain: Damage to the frontal micturition center (e.g., parasagittal meningioma, normal pressure hydrocephalus, ACA stroke) removes cortical inhibition over Barrington's nucleus, causing urge urinary incontinence.

open.q: How does the Pontine Micturition Center (Barrington's nucleus) coordinate detrusor contraction with urethral sphincter relaxation during voiding?
accept: Excites sacral (S2-S4) parasympathetic pelvic neurons to contract the detrusor while inhibiting sympathetic (hypogastric) and somatic pudendal (Onuf's nucleus) outflow to relax the internal and external urethral sphincters
Stimulates sacral parasympathetic detrusor contraction and inhibits sympathetic/pudendal sphincter contraction

questions.q: What is 'Wilson's disease' (hepatolenticular degeneration), and which basal ganglia structures are preferentially damaged?
options: Autosomal recessive mutation in the ATP7B copper-transporting ATPase gene causing impaired biliary copper excretion and ceruloplasmin incorporation; copper accumulates in the liver, cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings), and lentiform nucleus (putamen and globus pallidus), producing Parkinsonism, dystonia, wing-beating tremor, dysarthria, and psychiatric changes
Autoimmune demyelination of the optic nerve
Iron accumulation in the spinal dorsal columns
Excessive vitamin D deposition in the cerebellum
questions.explain: Copper deposition causes cystic degeneration of the putamen and globus pallidus (lentiform nucleus), treated with copper chelators (penicillamine, trientine) and oral zinc.

open.q: State the mutated gene, accumulated metal, and primary basal ganglia structures damaged in Wilson's disease.
accept: ATP7B gene; copper; lentiform nucleus (putamen and globus pallidus)
ATP7B; copper; putamen and globus pallidus (lentiform nucleus)

questions.q: Why do antipsychotic (neuroleptic) drugs such as haloperidol cause 'drug-induced Parkinsonism' acutely and 'tardive dyskinesia' after months to years of use?
options: Acute D2 receptor blockade in the striatum removes dopaminergic inhibition of the indirect pathway (mimicking Parkinson's disease); chronic D2 blockade induces compensatory upregulation and supersensitivity of striatal D2 receptors, causing hyperkinetic choreoathetoid oro-facial movements (tardive dyskinesia)
Haloperidol destroys the cerebellar dentate nucleus
Tardive dyskinesia is caused by acute D1 receptor destruction
Haloperidol increases striatal dopamine release by 1,000%
questions.explain: Recognizing D2 antagonism (acute hypokinetic Parkinsonism) vs chronic D2 receptor supersensitivity (late hyperkinetic tardive dyskinesia) directly illustrates basal ganglia D2 physiology.

open.q: Contrast the striatal D2 receptor mechanisms underlying acute neuroleptic-induced Parkinsonism versus chronic tardive dyskinesia.
accept: Acute Parkinsonism: direct D2 receptor blockade over-activates the indirect pathway; Tardive dyskinesia: chronic D2 blockade triggers compensatory D2 receptor upregulation and supersensitivity, over-suppressing the indirect pathway and causing involuntary movements
Acute D2 receptor antagonism (Parkinsonism) vs chronic D2 receptor upregulation/supersensitivity (tardive dyskinesia)

questions.q: How do 'fasciculus gracilis' and 'fasciculus cuneatus' differ in their spinal cord levels of origin and anatomical presence?
options: Fasciculus gracilis carries sensory afferents from the lower limbs and lower trunk (below T6) and is present throughout the ENTIRE length of the spinal cord (medial dorsal column); fasciculus cuneatus carries afferents from the upper trunk, upper limbs, and neck (T6 and above) and is present ONLY in the upper thoracic and cervical spinal cord (lateral dorsal column)
Fasciculus cuneatus is present in the sacral cord and carries toe sensation
Fasciculus gracilis is located in the anterior horn
Both fasciculi carry motor axons to skeletal muscle
questions.explain: A transverse section of the lumbar spinal cord shows ONLY the fasciculus gracilis in the dorsal funiculus, whereas a cervical section shows both gracilis (medial) and cuneatus (lateral).

open.q: Compare the body regions represented and spinal cord levels where fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus are found.
accept: Fasciculus gracilis: lower body/legs (below T6), present at all spinal levels medially; Fasciculus cuneatus: upper body/arms (T6 and above), present only in upper thoracic and cervical levels laterally
Lower body/all levels medially (gracilis) vs upper body/T6 and above laterally (cuneatus)

questions.sub: Brainstem Anatomy, Cranial Nerve Nuclei, and Rule of 4s
questions.q: What is 'Wallenberg's lateral medullary syndrome' dysphagia mechanism, and why does the uvula deviate AWAY from the side of a unilateral vagus/nucleus ambiguus lesion?
options: Lesion of the nucleus ambiguus paralyzes the ipsilateral levator veli palatini and pharyngeal constrictors; when the patient says 'ahh,' the intact contralateral palatal muscles pull the uvula AWAY from the paralyzed lesioned side (whereas a hypoglossal CN XII lesion causes the tongue to deviate TOWARD the lesioned side)
Both the uvula and tongue deviate toward the intact side
Both the uvula and tongue deviate away from the lesion
The uvula is innervated by the optic nerve
questions.explain: Classic board contrast: Palate/uvula deviates AWAY from a CN X/nucleus ambiguus lesion (pulled by intact contralateral muscles), whereas protruded tongue deviates TOWARD a CN XII lesion (pushed by intact contralateral genioglossus).

open.q: State the direction of deviation (toward vs away from the lesion) for: (1) the uvula in a unilateral CN X/nucleus ambiguus lesion and (2) the protruded tongue in a unilateral CN XII lesion.
accept: 1) Uvula deviates AWAY from the lesioned side; 2) Protruded tongue deviates TOWARD the lesioned side
Uvula away from lesion; tongue toward lesion

questions.q: A 48-year-old vegan woman presents with progressive paresthesias in her feet, unsteady gait worse in the dark, loss of vibration and joint position sense in both lower limbs, brisk 3+ patellar reflexes, bilateral extensor plantar (Babinski) responses, and macrocytic anemia (MCV 118 fL) with hypersegmented neutrophils. What is the diagnosis and neuroanatomical localization?
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord due to Vitamin B12 deficiency affecting the bilateral dorsal columns and bilateral lateral corticospinal tracts
Anterior spinal artery infarction
Tabes dorsalis from tertiary syphilis
Cerebellar vermis astrocytoma
questions.explain: Simultaneous dorsal column loss (vibration/proprioception loss, sensory ataxia) and UMN corticospinal signs (hyperreflexia, Babinski) in a patient with megaloblastic anemia is classic for B12 deficiency.

open.q: Identify the vitamin deficiency and the two spinal cord tracts damaged in a patient presenting with macrocytic anemia, loss of vibration/proprioception, and bilateral Babinski signs.
accept: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency (subacute combined degeneration); bilateral dorsal columns and bilateral lateral corticospinal tracts
Vitamin B12 deficiency; dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts

questions.q: A 63-year-old man develops sudden-onset right-sided facial droop (involving both forehead and lower face), right-sided sensorineural hearing loss, severe vertigo, nausea, right limb ataxia, right Horner syndrome, loss of pain and temperature on the right face and left body, and loss of the right corneal reflex. Which brainstem artery is occluded?
options: Right Anterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (AICA) — Lateral Pontine Syndrome
Right Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA)
Left Anterior Spinal Artery
Right Middle Cerebral Artery
questions.explain: Lateral pontine (AICA) stroke shares spinothalamic, spinal trigeminal, vestibular, cerebellar peduncle, and sympathetic features with PICA stroke, but adds ipsilateral CN VII (facial paralysis) and CN VIII (deafness via labyrinthine/internal auditory artery).

open.q: Which brainstem artery and region are infarcted when a stroke produces ipsilateral LMN facial paralysis, ipsilateral deafness, vertigo, ipsilateral ataxia, Horner syndrome, and crossed pain/temperature loss?
accept: Anterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (AICA); lateral caudal pons (Lateral Pontine Syndrome)
AICA / lateral pons

questions.q: A 38-year-old man with a family history of early-onset dementia and suicide develops involuntary, irregular, dance-like writhing movements of his fingers, face, and shoulders (chorea), impulsive behavior, and progressive memory loss. Brain MRI demonstrates marked bilateral atrophy of the heads of the caudate nuclei with secondary enlargement ('boxcar' appearance) of the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles. What is the diagnosis?
options: Huntington's disease (autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene on chromosome 4)
Idiopathic Parkinson's disease
Wilson's disease
Friedrich's ataxia
questions.explain: Atrophy of the caudate nucleus head flattens the normally convex lateral wall of the frontal horn of the lateral ventricle ('boxcar ventricles').

open.q: Which basal ganglia nucleus undergoes marked atrophy producing 'boxcar' enlargement of the lateral ventricles on MRI in Huntington's disease?
accept: Caudate nucleus (head of the caudate nucleus)
Caudate nucleus

questions.q: A 14-year-old boy with a germinoma of the pineal gland presents with headache, papilledema, inability to look upward, pupils that fail to constrict to direct light yet constrict briskly when focusing on a near object (light-near dissociation), and convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted upward gaze. What is this syndrome and how does the tumor cause papilledema?
options: Parinaud (dorsal midbrain) syndrome; the pineal tumor compresses the cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius, causing non-communicating obstructive hydrocephalus of the third and lateral ventricles
Wallenberg syndrome; occlusion of the vertebral artery
Weber syndrome; occlusion of the posterior communicating artery
Brown-Sequard syndrome; cervical disc herniation
questions.explain: Pineal region masses sit immediately dorsal to the midbrain tectum and cerebral aqueduct, compressing vertical gaze centers (Parinaud syndrome) and obstructing CSF outflow from the third to fourth ventricle.

open.q: Explain how a pineal gland tumor causes both upward gaze palsy and obstructive hydrocephalus.
accept: It compresses the dorsal midbrain pretectal area/superior colliculi (producing Parinaud upward gaze palsy) and obstructs the adjacent cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius (causing non-communicating hydrocephalus)
Compression of dorsal midbrain vertical gaze centers and obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman undergoes a radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection, and later sustains a stab wound to the left back at T10 causing left-sided spastic monoplegia of the left leg, loss of vibration and proprioception in the left foot, and loss of pain and temperature over the entire right leg from T12 downward. Why is pain and temperature preserved at T10 and T11 on the right side?
options: Second-order spinothalamic axons ascend 1 to 2 spinal segments ipsilaterally in Lissauer's tract before decussating in the anterior white commissure, so fibers entering at T10 and T11 have not yet crossed at the T10 lesion level
T10 and T11 dermatomes have no pain receptors
Spinothalamic fibers cross in the medulla oblongata
The left dorsal columns carry pain from the right T10 dermatome
questions.explain: This 1-2 segment offset between the level of the spinal hemisection and the contralateral spinothalamic sensory level is a classic neuroanatomical localization rule.

open.q: Why does a unilateral spinal cord hemisection at T10 produce contralateral loss of pain and temperature starting at T11-T12 rather than T10?
accept: Primary nociceptive afferents ascend 1 to 2 segments in Lissauer's tract before synapsing and crossing in the anterior white commissure, so T10-T11 fibers cross above the T10 lesion
Incoming pain fibers ascend 1-2 segments in Lissauer's tract before decussating

questions.q: A 45-year-old man with severe bilateral lower back pain after a heavy lifting injury develops numbness over his buttocks and perineum ('saddle anesthesia'), inability to void urine, loss of anal sphincter tone, severe asymmetric weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and plantar flexion, and absent bilateral Achilles reflexes. Emergency lumbar MRI shows a massive central L4-L5 disc extrusion. What is the diagnosis and urgency?
options: Cauda equina syndrome — a neurosurgical emergency requiring urgent surgical decompression within 24-48 hours to prevent permanent sphincter and motor paralysis
Benign piriformis muscle strain treated with 6 weeks of bed rest
Conus medullaris infarction at C4
Lateral medullary syndrome
questions.explain: Because the spinal cord ends at L1-L2, a massive central L4-L5 disc herniation compresses multiple lumbosacral nerve roots in the cauda equina, requiring emergent laminectomy/discectomy.

open.q: Identify the neurosurgical emergency indicated by acute saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, asymmetric lower-limb LMN weakness, and absent ankle jerks subsequent to a large central L4-L5 disc herniation.
accept: Cauda equina syndrome
Cauda equina compression syndrome

questions.q: A 66-year-old man suffers a large right cerebral hemisphere stroke. In the ICU, his level of consciousness deteriorates and he exhibits sustained flexion of his left elbow, wrist, and fingers with rigid extension and internal rotation of his left leg ('decorticate posturing'). Six hours later, his right pupil dilates to 7 mm and BOTH upper and lower limbs become rigidly extended ('decerebrate posturing'). What anatomical progression occurred?
options: Transtentorial (uncal/central) brain herniation compressed the ipsilateral CN III (dilated pupil) and progressed downward to damage the midbrain at or below the red nucleus, eliminating rubrospinal flexor drive and leaving unopposed vestibulospinal/pontine reticulospinal extensor tone
His stroke resolved spontaneously and motor function recovered
He developed a peripheral radial nerve palsy in the left arm
Cerebellar Purkinje cells began firing at 1,000 Hz
questions.explain: Transition from decorticate (lesion above red nucleus) to decerebrate posturing (lesion at/below red nucleus) accompanied by ipsilateral CN III mydriasis signals life-threatening downward transtentorial herniation.

open.q: What clinical event is signaled when a comatose stroke patient transitions from decorticate posturing to decerebrate posturing with an ipsilateral dilated pupil?
accept: Downward transtentorial (uncal/central) brain herniation compressing CN III and progressing to midbrain dysfunction at or below the red nucleus
Downward transtentorial herniation damaging the midbrain at or below the red nucleus

questions.q: A 59-year-old woman with severe chronic schizophrenia treated with high-dose haloperidol for 12 years develops continuous involuntary lip-smacking, tongue protrusion, chewing movements, and choreiform finger movements ('tardive dyskinesia'). Which neurotransmitter mechanism explains this condition?
options: Chronic blockade of striatal D2 dopamine receptors induces compensatory D2 receptor upregulation and supersensitivity, over-inhibiting the indirect pathway and disinhibiting thalamocortical motor drive
Complete destruction of the cerebellar vermis
Acute acetylcholine toxicity at the neuromuscular junction
Deficiency of vitamin B12 in the dorsal columns
questions.explain: Tardive dyskinesia is treated by tapering/switching to an atypical antipsychotic (e.g., clozapine, quetiapine) or prescribing a VMAT2 inhibitor (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) to reduce presynaptic vesicular dopamine release.

open.q: What receptor adaptation in the basal ganglia causes tardive dyskinesia after years of typical antipsychotic therapy?
accept: Upregulation and supersensitivity of striatal D2 dopamine receptors following chronic D2 antagonism
Striatal D2 receptor upregulation / supersensitivity

questions.q: A 16-year-old boy presents with progressive gait ataxia, dysarthria, loss of vibration and position sense in his legs, absent deep tendon reflexes, extensor plantar (Babinski) responses, pes cavus (high-arched feet), kyphoscoliosis, diabetes mellitus, and concentric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Genetic testing shows an autosomal recessive GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the frataxin (FXN) gene on chromosome 9. What is the diagnosis?
options: Friedreich's ataxia (degeneration of spinocerebellar tracts, dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal tracts, and dorsal root ganglia)
Huntington's disease
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Myasthenia gravis
questions.explain: Friedreich's ataxia impairs mitochondrial iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis (frataxin), causing combined degeneration of spinocerebellar tracts, dorsal columns, and corticospinal tracts alongside hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (the most common cause of death).

open.q: Name the inherited ataxia caused by a GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the frataxin gene and list the three major spinal cord tracts it degenerates.
accept: Friedreich's ataxia; spinocerebellar tracts, dorsal columns, and lateral corticospinal tracts
Friedreich's ataxia; spinocerebellar, dorsal column, and corticospinal tracts

questions.q: A 56-year-old man presents with progressive asymmetric hand weakness, muscle cramps, fasciculations in his tongue and deltoids, severe atrophy of his thenar muscles, AND brisk 4+ patellar reflexes with bilateral Babinski signs. Sensation, eye movements, and bowel/bladder function are completely normal. Which motor neurons are degenerating?
options: Combined degeneration of BOTH Upper Motor Neurons (betz cells/corticospinal & corticobulbar tracts) AND Lower Motor Neurons (ventral horn alpha motor neurons & brainstem motor nuclei) — Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS / Lou Gehrig's disease)
Isolated degeneration of dorsal root ganglia
Isolated degeneration of substantia nigra pars compacta
Autoimmune destruction of Schwann cell myelin only
questions.explain: Coexistence of LMN signs (atrophy, fasciculations) and UMN signs (hyperreflexia, spasticity, Babinski) in the same limb with spared sensory, ocular, and sphincter functions is diagnostic of ALS.

open.q: Which two motor neuron populations degenerate in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), and which neurological systems remain characteristically spared?
accept: Both Upper Motor Neurons (corticospinal/corticobulbar) and Lower Motor Neurons (ventral horn and bulbar motor neurons) degenerate; sensory pathways, extraocular muscles, and bowel/bladder sphincters (Onuf's nucleus) are spared
UMN and LMN degeneration; sensory, oculomotor, and sphincter functions spared
